facts.fact: Thread (filamentous) algae are colonies of single-celled algae joined into long green threads.
Filamentous algae is a group that includes hair, staghorn, string and thread algae. Pulled out of the tank, it looks like wet hair.
Blue-green 'algae' (cyanobacteria) are bacteria, not true algae.
Green water is caused by free-floating single-celled organisms (Euglena) that cloud the water.
The goal should be to keep algae at a safe level, not to wipe it out 100%.
Black beard algae (BBA, rêu chùm đen) is called the hardest nuisance algae to treat.
Black brush/beard algae (Rhodophyta) is a black, brown, red or green coating that can quickly cover plants and hardscape.
Rêu chùm đen grows in black, dark green or dark red tufts and favours strong water flow.
BBA is black or grey and grips tightly to rocks, driftwood and leaf edges.
Staghorn algae (Compsopogon sp.) is coarse, branching strands like antlers, in white, grey or green, on leaves and equipment.
Rêu sừng hươu is grey-green and branching. It often appears where flow is strong, such as at the filter outlet.
Brown algae (diatoms) form a brown, muddy film on leaves and hardscape. They are rare in established tanks.
Tảo nâu (diatoms) is a brown slimy layer on glass, rocks and driftwood that wipes off easily.
Cyanobacteria form green, black or purple slime with an 'earthy' smell.
Rêu nhớt (cyanobacteria) forms a thick, mat-like layer with gas bubbles underneath. It is dark green in freshwater and dark red in saltwater.
Rêu nhớt xanh smells pungent.
Cladophora forms tough, green, wool-like mats, often in hairgrass, substrate and hardscape.
Fuzz algae shows as slightly fuzzy edges on plant leaves.
Rêu lông tơ shows as short threads, about 2 cm long, on leaf edges, mostly in brightly lit tanks.
Green dust algae (GDA) is a dusty green film on the glass that usually avoids hardscape and leaves.
Green spot algae (Choleochaete orbicularis) appears on glass and on long-lived leaves such as Java fern, Anubias and Bolbitis.
Hair/thread algae has long green filaments up to 30cm, often tangled in moss.

White 'algae' (rêu trắng) is fungus or bacteria. The fungal form is cottony and grows on leftover food or new driftwood. The bacterial form is a thin film over substrate, plants and rocks after setup.
Green water is normally caused by too high nutrient concentrations in the water.
Blue-green coatings usually appear only from excessive feeding.
Filamentous algae is linked to excess nutrients such as iron, too much light, or too few nutrients for a long lighting period.
Hair/thread algae is linked to iron above 0.15ppm.
BBA is linked to nutrient imbalance (possibly excess N, P, Fe). Low pH is a suspected cause, only 'believed' rather than proven.
Staghorn is linked to nutrient imbalance and low CO2.
Diatoms are linked to new setups, excess silica and possibly old bulbs.
Cyanobacteria are linked to low nitrate, high organics from overfeeding, old bulbs and poor circulation.
Green spot algae appears almost exclusively when phosphate (PO4) is depleted.
Cladophora can be brought in with Marimo balls.
Green water can follow a new setup, a nutrient imbalance, or medication that damages the biofilter.
Spirogyra often appears about 2 weeks after setup, while the nitrogen cycle is still unstable, from excess light and nutrients.
Light is a main driver: lights on too long, too strong, or not made for planted tanks.
Rêu trắng does not photosynthesise, so cutting light does not help. It feeds on leftover food and waste, and poor flow lets it settle.
Pull filamentous algae out by hand, using a toothbrush on large clumps.
Shorten the lighting period when filamentous algae appears.
Bleach dip for BBA or staghorn on hardscape and hardy plants: 1:20 bleach to water, then rinse until there is no bleach smell before returning items to the tank.
Spot-treat BBA with Excel or H2O2 from a syringe, then remove it by hand once it turns grey/white.
Copper algaecides will most likely also kill aquarium plants. GWAPA does not recommend them.
For cyanobacteria: raise nitrate to about 5ppm, black out the tank, and add fast-growing plants.
Erythromycin at half dosage (Maracyn) is used against cyanobacteria without harming most plants.
For green spot algae, raise PO4 to 0.5-2.0ppm and scrape the glass with a razor blade.
Green dust algae can be left alone. It should harden and fall off after roughly 21 days, then scrape the rest and do a thorough clean and water change.
For green water: blackout for 5 days plus small 5-10% water changes daily until clear. A UV sterilizer, micron filter, flocculant or Daphnia also help.
After a 5-day blackout, plants may look a little ratty for a week or so.
Most fish and invertebrates will not eat staghorn algae.
Amano shrimp are the main control for thread algae. Up to 2 shrimps per 5 L of water may be needed for a transitional period.
Tropica generally advises against removing thread algae with chemicals, because some products harm aquarium plants.
Tropica does not recommend UV as a standard aid against green water, because the UV light also kills useful bacteria.
Seachem's test on Vallisneria: no problems at the recommended Excel dose. At double dose some leaves melted, but new leaves grew back strongly.
Seachem says Excel damage to vals is temporary because roots are not affected. Dosing N, P, Fe and K alongside lets vals take much higher Excel levels without melting.
One method: mix H2O2 50:50 with water and inject it into the worst algae. Turn the filter off for a few hours, then change 50% of the water the next day. Repeat if needed, but do not overuse.
For BBA, inject 3% H2O2 directly into the algae with a syringe. The source gives roughly 1 ml per 2 litres of water.
Diatoms in a new tank usually go away in 4-6 weeks as the tank settles, or can be scrubbed off.
For diatoms, check or replace the lights and change 30-50% of the water repeatedly until they are gone. Otocinclus help.
Whole-tank H2O2 dose: 1.5ml of 3% hydrogen peroxide per 1 gallon of true water volume (minus substrate and decor).
H2O2 kills nitrifying bacteria. Take the filter out and run it in saved tank water during treatment, and check ammonia afterwards.
No published experiments measure how much H2O2 dwarf shrimp can take. Overdosing can kill shrimp, and baby shrimp are less resistant.
If shrimp show distress after H2O2, dose 2-3 times the normal water conditioner amount to neutralise the peroxide.
The Shrimp Farm does not recommend H2O2 for purely cosmetic algae. For BBA it prefers scrubbing by hand.
Algae eaters: otocinclus for soft algae and diatoms, Siamese algae eater for BBA and staghorn, Amano shrimp for hair algae, nerite snails for hard algae on glass.
Nerite snails clear green spot algae from leaves and glass.
Step 1: identify the algae type, because each type has different causes and treatments.
Step 2: remove algae by hand (toothbrush, tweezers, scraper) and trim badly covered or old leaves.
Step 3: do weekly to bi-weekly water changes and rebalance nutrients and CO2.
Step 4: spot-treat stubborn BBA, staghorn or Cladophora with Excel or H2O2.
Step 5: add a suitable cleanup crew for the algae type.
Nutrient targets: N 10-20ppm, P 0.5-2ppm, K 10-20ppm, Ca 10-30ppm, Mg 2-5ppm, Fe 0.1ppm. CO2 20-30ppm as livestock allow.
Light 6-8 hours/day, or 5-6 hours/day for a new tank. It can be split into 2-3 periods of 3-4 hours each.
Light 8-10 hours/day, or 4-6 hours for a new tank.
Keep CO2 at 20-30 ppm, checked with a drop checker (green means correct).
Filter flow should be 5-7 times tank volume (a 100 litre tank needs 500-700 litres/hour).
Water changes: 2-3 times a week in the first month. In a stable tank, 20-30% per week.
Water changes: 20% 2-3 times a week in a new tank, 10-15% daily in a stable tank.
Feeding less usually makes blue-green algae disappear again.
Do not let nitrate drop to zero, since that triggers cyanobacteria.
Overdosing algae chemicals to get quick results stresses fish, weakens plants and upsets the bacteria.
Turning lights off for many days to 'kill' algae is listed as a mistake.
Changing too much water, or changing it too suddenly, is a common error.
Treating only the symptom without finding the cause lets algae come back.
Siamese algae eaters (cá bút chì) and cá nô lệ eat nuisance algae at first, but later eat decorative moss and damage plants.
Scraping green dust algae early may interrupt its lifecycle and delay clearing.
Large water changes against green water stop helpful microorganisms from establishing.
Without fixing water quality and excess nutrients first, algae will likely return after H2O2 treatment.

Vietnamese hobbyists use these names: rêu chùm đen (BBA), rêu sừng hươu (staghorn), rêu tóc (hair algae), tảo nâu (diatoms), rêu nhớt/rêu lam (cyanobacteria), rêu đốm xanh (green spot), rêu bụi xanh (GDA), rêu lông tơ (fuzz), nước xanh (green water).
Vietnamese names for algae eaters include cá bút chì (Siamese algae eater), tép Yamato/Amano, cá otto and ốc Nerite.
Cheap local algae eaters recommended include mún đỏ, cá hòa lan, cá hắc culy, tép mồi and tép RC.
Outdoor tanks get algae back more easily because of direct sun.
Strong light, often from sun on outdoor tanks, is the main cause of green water (rêu nước xanh).
Keep direct sunlight off the tank, and use dechlorinated or RO water.
Products sold in Vietnam for algae include Seachem Excel, JBL Algol and ADA Phyton Git (herbal, gentler).
Hair algae eaters named in Vietnamese include tép Amano, tép mũi đỏ, tép Thanh Mai, ốc Nerita and cá bút chì.
GWAPA says the idea that low pH causes BBA is a belief, not established fact.
GWAPA says expecting fish or invertebrates to control staghorn is wrong, since most will not eat it.
Diatom growth is tied to silica. Check silica levels with your water utility.
Cladophora is hard to remove completely and can be left if it is not a problem.
